opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different things that make me somewhat hopeful, though I want to caveat upfront that I'm not, like, super optimistic overall. I think the situation is pretty precarious.

But one thing that gives me hope is that I think there's a lot of relatively cheap, tractable work that could substantially reduce risk, even in worlds where we don't get a ton of political will or a ton of time. A lot of my work has been on AI control: the idea that even if you can't be confident your models aren't scheming against you, you can set up protocols, monitoring, restricted affordances, auditing, and so on, so that even if the model *is* trying to subvert your safety measures, it's hard for it to cause a catastrophe. What's nice about control is that it's somewhat more evaluable than alignment. You can run red-team/blue-team exercises where the red team plays the role of a misaligned model and you measure whether your protocol catches it. That gives you an empirical feedback loop, which is a lot of what you want in a research field.

The second thing is that we're going to have pretty capable AI systems that can help us do safety research. If we can get to the point where we have AIs that are roughly as capable as top human researchers, and we can use them in a way where we're reasonably confident they aren't sabotaging us, then the amount of safety labor available could go up enormously. Maybe there's a window where we have very capable but not wildly superhuman systems, and if we use that window well, we could make a lot of progress on problems that currently look hard, like interpretability, or figuring out whether models are actually aligned rather than just looking aligned.

Third, I think it matters a lot what the default trajectory looks like versus a moderately careful one. You don't need everything to go perfectly. If the leading AI developers spend even a modest fraction of their compute and staff on safety, take misalignment risk seriously as a threat model, and are willing to slow down somewhat at critical points, I think that meaningfully cuts risk. Research now helps make those interventions shovel-ready, so that when people are willing to act, they actually know what to do.

And then there's understanding the problem better. A big part of the value of research right now is just getting evidence. If we can produce clear demonstrations of models doing things like alignment faking, or reasoning about deceiving their overseers, that can shift how seriously people take the risk. And if it turns out things are easier than we feared, that's also really valuable to know.

So I'd put it as: the problem is hard, timelines might be short, and I don't think we're on track to handle it well by default. But there's a lot of low-hanging fruit, and the marginal value of careful work right now seems really high.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the default trajectory with a moderately careful one, where developers devote some compute and staff to safety and may slow down at critical points.

r002.rationale: It points to tractable work and low-hanging fruit that could reduce risk, but does not clearly say that incremental refinement could improve the situation over eight years without major conceptual breakthroughs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things. The first is just that the models we have now are actually pretty useful for doing research, and that's going to keep improving. So a lot of the alignment work that previously would have taken a human research team months, you can start to imagine AIs doing a big chunk of it, and then eventually most of it. If we can get to a point where we're able to safely use AIs to do alignment research, then the amount of work we can do in a given period of time goes up a lot. I'm not saying that's guaranteed to work out, but it's one of the main things I'm optimistic about.

The second thing is that I think a lot of the most important stuff is fairly low-tech. It's things like having good oversight of what the AIs are doing, having control measures in place so that even if the model is misaligned, it can't do something catastrophic, having decent monitoring, and then also just having better evaluations so you can tell when things are starting to go wrong. A lot of that is not deep science, it's more like engineering and institutional stuff. And I think that's actually tractable on a timescale of a few years, where some of the more fundamental questions about understanding what's going on inside the model might not be.

And then the third thing is, I think the field has gotten a lot more concrete. A few years ago, a lot of alignment research was pretty abstract, and it was hard to know if what you were doing was making any difference. Now we have models that actually exhibit the behaviors we're worried about in some form, so you can run experiments. You can test whether models try to deceive you, whether they behave differently when they think they're being observed, that kind of thing. That makes it much easier to make progress, and it also makes it easier to convince people that the problems are real, which matters a lot for getting the resources and the policy support you need.

I think the thing I'd caveat is that I don't think safety research alone is going to be enough. You also need the labs and governments to actually act on it, and you need some amount of time. If things go extremely fast, that's harder. But conditional on having something like eight years, and on people taking it seriously, I think we could end up in a materially better position than we're in now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts improving model usefulness with safety progress that requires deliberately using AI for alignment research, building oversight and control measures, and getting labs and governments to act.

r002.rationale: It says practical oversight, controls, monitoring, and evaluations are tractable within a few years even if deeper questions remain unresolved, and that this could leave us materially better off over eight years.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is that there’s a lot we could do that we haven’t tried very hard to do yet. Eight years is a substantial amount of time to build up a science of how these systems behave, test interventions, and work out which safety measures actually hold up as models become more capable.

For example, you can study whether an AI can carry out some harmful action despite the safeguards around it. Can it evade monitoring? Can it undermine the process we’re using to evaluate it? You don’t need to solve every aspect of alignment to make progress on those questions. And if you find that a particular setup fails, you can change it and test again. That gives you a potentially useful feedback loop, though there’s still the difficult question of whether your tests capture the failures you’ll encounter in practice.

Another possibility is that increasingly capable AI systems help with the research itself. That isn’t automatically reassuring—you have to worry about trusting their work—but being able to get much more research done could make a substantial difference.

So I wouldn’t say that eight years of progress guarantees a good outcome. But I do think there are concrete research directions where additional effort could buy us meaningful reductions in risk. We’re uncertain about how hard the problem is, and that uncertainty leaves room for research to turn out to be very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes deliberate research effort but does not distinguish that from safety improvements that might occur by default.

r002.rationale: It describes repeatedly testing and refining safety setups, says major progress does not require solving every aspect of alignment, and suggests additional effort could meaningfully reduce risk over eight years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason for hope is that there are a lot of things we could try that seem like they might substantially reduce the risk, and we haven’t tried them very hard yet. That’s also an alarming fact about the current situation, but it means there could be considerable room for progress.

For example, you don’t necessarily have to solve the entire problem of making an AI reliably want what you want. You could also get better at evaluating whether it’s behaving dangerously, restricting what it can do, and using other AI systems to monitor its actions. None of those approaches is a complete solution, but they could buy us time or let us use powerful systems to help with further safety research.

And eight years is enough time to learn quite a lot, especially if we get better empirical evidence about the failure modes we’re worried about. I wouldn’t want to assume that progress will happen automatically. But I do think there are concrete research directions where additional effort could make a meaningful difference, even if the underlying alignment problem turns out to be very hard.

r001.rationale: The response says promising approaches have not yet been tried very hard, so progress depends on additional effort, and cautions that it will not happen automatically.

r002.rationale: It describes several partial techniques that could substantially reduce risk without solving the whole alignment problem, and says focused effort over eight years could make a meaningful difference.
